summary: This unit teaches you to give a safe gel nail service: check the lamp and the products, consult with the client and look for contraindications, prepare the natural nail, apply gel polish and builder gel (including over tips), cure each layer correctly, finish and check the nails, give aftercare advice and carry out maintenance and safe removal. Preventing allergy and burns from the lamp and the product runs through every step.

blocks.p: Gel nail enhancement uses gels that stay soft until they are hardened ('cured') under a nail lamp. Gel polish gives a thin, glossy colour that lasts for weeks. Builder gel is thicker and is used to strengthen the nail or to build length over tips. This unit is for GENERAL BEAUTY THERAPY LEVEL 2 trainees.

Gel looks simple, but it has its own risks. Uncured gel on the skin is the most common cause of allergy among nail technicians and clients. A lamp that does not match the gel leaves product half-cured. Thick layers can burn. So this unit is about **control of the gel, the lamp and the skin contact** as much as a neat finish.

sections.title: The gel system: products, lamps and curing

blocks.p: Gel is a thick liquid made of small molecules. It also contains a **photoinitiator**, a chemical that reacts to light of a certain kind. When the right light shines on the gel, the photoinitiator starts a reaction that joins the molecules into a hard plastic. This is **curing**. Gel does not dry by evaporation, and it will not harden by itself in the pot or in the room. It needs the right lamp.

head: Gel
What it is
How it comes off
rows: Soft (soak-off) gel and gel polish
Thinner and more flexible. Gel polish gives colour; soft builder gel adds a little strength.
Soaks off in acetone
Hard gel
Thicker and harder; used for strong overlays and for length.
Cannot be soaked off properly: it is filed off
Builder gel
A thick gel used to build an apex and add strength or length. It may be soft (soak-off) or hard, so check the label.
As its label says

blocks.h: The layers of a gel service

head: Layer
What it does
Notes
rows: Bonder or primer (some systems)
Helps the gel stick to the natural nail.
Used only as the maker says; keep off the skin.
Base coat
A thin first layer that grips the nail and protects it from colour.
Cure it. It keeps a slightly tacky surface so that the next layer bonds.
Colour coat(s)
Gives the colour. Usually two thin coats.
Cure each coat. Thick colour can wrinkle or cause a heat spike.
Builder gel
Builds strength and shape; forms the apex.
Thin first layer, then the bead; cure as the maker says.
Top coat
A glossy final layer that seals and protects.
Cap the free edge. A 'no-wipe' top coat leaves no sticky layer.
Cleanser and lint-free wipe
Remove the sticky layer after the final cure.
Cleanser usually contains alcohol: it is flammable.
Cuticle oil
Moisturises the skin after the service.
Applied last.

blocks.p: Gel exposed to air does not cure on its very top, because oxygen interferes. This leaves a slightly sticky film called the **inhibition layer** (the sticky layer). It helps the next layer to bond, so you do **not** wipe it off between layers. You wipe it off only after the **final** cure of top coat or builder, with cleanser on a lint-free wipe.

head: Lamp
How it works
Typical cure time
rows: UV lamp (fluorescent bulbs)
Gives mostly UVA light. Many gels were first made for these.
Often about 2 minutes per layer
LED lamp (light emitting diode)
Gives a narrow band of light from small lights. Cures faster; the lights last longer.
Often 30 to 60 seconds per layer
UV/LED (dual) lamp
Gives both kinds of light.
As the maker of the gel says

ul: A gel's photoinitiator responds to certain light. A gel made for UV may not cure fully in an LED-only lamp, and the reverse. Always use the lamp the **gel maker** recommends, and cure for the time given for that gel and that lamp.
Lamp strength is shown in watts, but more watts is not always better: the right match with the gel matters more.
Clean the lamp, check the cord and plug, and make sure every bulb or LED lights before the client sits down.
UV bulbs weaken with age, even though they still light up, so they must be replaced as the maker says. A weak lamp leaves gel under-cured.
Do not mix gels from different makers in one set. They may not cure or bond well together.

blocks.p: Gel that is **under-cured** has not fully hardened. It may feel soft, wrinkle, lift, or leave uncured product against the skin. It is a main cause of allergy. Causes: layers too thick, the wrong lamp, an old bulb, too short a cure time, or a hand not placed properly in the lamp.

blocks.note: In Jamaica, power cuts and voltage changes happen. If the lamp switches off partway through a cure, the layer is not cured. Wait until the power is back, then cure again for the full time. Do not wipe off or file gel that has not cured fully.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Working safely: the lamp, the gel and the skin

head: Hazard
Risk
How you control it
rows: Light from the lamp
Strong light can harm the eyes; UV adds to skin ageing and sun damage
Do not look into the lamp
Cure for the maker's time only
Fingerless UV-protective gloves, or broad-spectrum sunscreen on the hands, for UV lamps
Heat during curing
A sudden burning feeling (heat spike), worse with thick gel or thin nails
Thin layers
Flash cure first when the maker says
Take the hand out briefly if it burns
Uncured gel on skin
Allergy (sensitisation), which can last for life
Keep a small gap at the skin
Clean spills before curing
Do not touch uncured gel; change gloves when soiled
Gel cleanser and acetone
Flammable; dry the skin; irritating vapour
Keep away from heat and flames; keep lids closed
Ventilate; protect skin
Filing dust
Irritates eyes, nose, throat and skin; carries cured gel dust
Desk extraction on
Dust mask and safety glasses
Brush or wipe dust away; never blow it
Electrical equipment
Shock; overheating
Check cords and plugs; keep cables clear and dry
Report and stop using any faulty lamp
Posture and light
Back, neck, wrist and eye strain
Good light, a chair at the right height, regular breaks

blocks.h: Protecting the eyes and skin from the lamp

ul: Neither you nor the client should look straight into the lamp. Place the hand so that you are not looking into the light.
Offer fingerless UV gloves or sunscreen on the hands. Apply it before the service and let it dry. This protects the skin on the back of the hand and fingers.

Some medicines, and some skin conditions, make the skin more sensitive to light. Ask about this in the consultation. If she takes such a medicine, ask her to check with her doctor before you use a UV lamp.

blocks.p: When gel cures it gives off heat. If the layer is thick, if there is a lot of pigment, if the lamp is very strong, or if the natural nail is thin, the heat can build quickly and feel like a sudden burn. This is a **heat spike**.

flow: Client says it is burning
Take the hand out of the lamp at once
Wait a few seconds, then put the hand back and finish the cure
Make later layers thinner, and flash cure first
Record it if it was severe

ul: Do not make the client 'tough it out'. A heat spike will not hurt the nail if the hand is taken out in time.
A **flash cure** is a short cure of a few seconds that holds the gel in place and lets it harden a little before the full cure.
Thin the layers: it is the best way to avoid a heat spike.

blocks.p: Gels contain acrylate chemicals. When uncured gel touches the skin again and again, the body can become sensitive to it. This is called **sensitisation**, and it usually lasts for life. After that, even a tiny touch can set off a reaction, and the person may react to other products with the same chemicals, including acrylic nails and some dental materials.

head: Who
Signs
rows: Client
Itching, redness or swelling of the skin around the nails
Blisters, dry cracked skin on the fingertips
Nails that lift or loosen
Itching or a rash on the eyelids or face from touching them with the hands
Nail technician
Itchy, dry, red or cracked fingertips and fingers
Rash on the face, neck or eyelids
Reaction that gets worse with every service

ul: **Prevention:** leave a small gap between the gel and the skin; clean spills before curing; use thin layers and cure fully with the right lamp and time; never mix makers; keep your own gloves and skin clean.

Gloves help but do **not** make it safe to touch gel. Uncured gel can pass through thin gloves, so aim never to touch uncured gel at all. Change gloves when soiled and do not touch your face with them.

**If a client shows signs:** stop, do not carry on, clean the product off the skin, record the reaction on her record card, tell your supervisor, and refer her to a doctor. No more gel services until a doctor has advised.
If **you** show signs, tell your supervisor and see a doctor. Sensitisation can end a nail technician's career.

head: What happened
What you do
rows: Uncured gel on the skin
Wipe it off at once with a lint-free wipe and a little cleanser or soap and water, then wash. Watch for redness or itching.
Gel, cleanser or acetone in the eye
Rinse with plenty of clean running water for several minutes. Get medical help. Record it.
Dizziness, headache or sore throat
Stop, get fresh air, give water, and check the ventilation and extraction.
Burn from the lamp or a heat spike that leaves a red or painful finger
Cool the finger in cool running water, and get medical help if it blisters.
Small fire
Switch off equipment, move flammable bottles if it is safe, and use the Centre's extinguisher as you were trained. Raise the alarm.

ul: Read the **safety data sheet (SDS)** and the maker's instructions for each product. The SDS lists hazards, first aid, storage and disposal.
Gel cleanser contains alcohol and acetone is a solvent. Both are **flammable**: no smoking, naked flames, candles, mosquito coils or heat near the desk.
Keep pots and bottles **closed**, out of direct sunlight and away from the lamp. Light can start curing the gel in the pot, which ruins the product.
In Jamaica's heat, keep gels in a cool place; never leave them in a hot car or on a sunny window ledge.
Store products in their own labelled containers. Never decant them into unlabelled bottles.
Wipes, cotton and foil with gel or cleanser on them go in a **lidded bin**, emptied every day.
Keep the brushes capped and out of the light. Wipe them clean after use, as the maker says.

blocks.note: No eating, drinking or smoking at the desk. Wash your hands before you eat. Extraction on whenever you file.
blocks.label: Safety

head: Word
What it means
At the nail desk
rows: Cleaning
Removing dirt, dust and product with detergent and water. It comes first.
Washing a cuticle pusher in warm, soapy water.
Disinfecting
Using a chemical at the maker's strength and for the full contact time to kill most germs.
Soaking a clean metal tool; wiping the desk.
Sterilising
Killing all germs, including spores, usually in an autoclave.
For some metal tools.
Contact time
How long a surface or tool must stay wet with disinfectant.
As the label says.

ul: Both technician and client wash their hands at the start, before any work on the nails.
Metal tools are cleaned, then disinfected as the maker says, dried and stored covered.
**Throw away** after one client: paper files and buffers, orange sticks and wipes. A file cannot be disinfected properly.
Wipe the desk with disinfectant, put out a fresh towel, and put used towels in a closed laundry bin.
Check the lamp: wipe it, check the cord and plug and make sure every bulb or LED lights. Do this **before** the client arrives, so that every layer will cure fully.

blocks.note: A UV cabinet only keeps tools that are already clean and disinfected clean while they are stored. It does not disinfect dirty tools.
blocks.label: Remember

flow: Greet the client and ask her to wash her hands
Ask your questions
Look at the hands and nails in good light
Check for contraindications
Agree the service, length, colour, time and price
Explain aftercare and maintenance
Complete the record card and get her signature

head: Ask about
Why it matters
rows: Past reactions to nail products, gloves or cosmetics
To spot an existing allergy. It is the most useful question for gel.
Medicines and skin conditions
Some make the skin more sensitive to light; some conditions slow healing.
Health: diabetes, circulation, pregnancy
Some conditions need a doctor's advice or extra care.
Her work, hobbies and nail habits
Wet work and knocks shorten the life of a set.
The look she wants: gel polish, overlay or length
Chooses the products and the method.
Previous enhancements and how they were removed
Damage from peeling or over-filing shows how gentle you must be.
Time and cost
Tell her the price in JMD and when an infill is due.

blocks.p: A **contraindication** is something that means the service must not go ahead, or must be changed. You are not a doctor: never name a disease as a fact, and never try to treat a condition. Describe what you see, explain tactfully, advise a doctor, and record it.

head: Condition
What you see or learn
What you do
rows: Infection of the skin fold (paronychia)
Red, swollen, painful skin by the nail, possibly with pus
Do not apply gel. Refer to a doctor.
Fungal infection of the nail (onychomycosis)
Thick, yellow or brown, crumbly nail
Do not apply gel. Refer to a doctor.
Nail plate lifting off the nail bed (onycholysis)
White or yellow area under a lifting nail
Do not apply gel over it. Refer if painful or repeated.
Warts or broken skin
Growths; cuts, grazes
Avoid the area; do not work on broken skin.
Eczema or psoriasis of the hands
Red, sore, scaly or cracked skin
Avoid affected areas; refer if the skin is inflamed.
Earlier allergy to gel or acrylic
Itching, redness or swelling after a previous service
Do not apply gel. Refer to a doctor. Record.
Medicine or condition that makes the skin sensitive to light
She tells you she takes such a medicine, or has a light-sensitive condition
Ask her to check with her doctor before using a UV lamp.
Diabetes or poor circulation
Slow healing, numb fingers
Ask her to check with her doctor first.

blocks.note: Record the consultation on her card, with the date, her answers, what you found, the product and the lamp used, and her **signed consent**. A client under 18 needs a parent's or guardian's consent. Keep records locked away: under Jamaica's Data Protection Act they are personal information.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Preparing the natural nail and fitting tips

blocks.h: Parts of the nail you need to know

head: Part
What it is
rows: Nail plate
The hard, visible part.
Nail bed
The skin under the plate.
Matrix
The root of the nail, where it is made.
Eponychium
The fold of living skin at the base of the nail.
Cuticle
A thin layer of dead skin on the nail plate.
Side walls
The folds of skin along each side.
Free edge
The part that grows past the end of the finger.
Hyponychium
The skin under the free edge that seals the nail bed.
Stress area
Where the nail leaves the nail bed; most breaks happen here.

blocks.p: Gel sticks to a clean, dry, lightly roughened nail. It does not stick to oil, dust, water or cuticle skin on the plate. Most lifting starts at this stage.

flow: Wash hands, and remove old polish
Push back the cuticle gently and remove dead skin from the nail plate
Shape the free edge
Lightly buff the shine off the nail plate with a fine file or buffer
Brush away the dust
Apply dehydrator to the nail plate
Apply bonder or primer to the nail plate if the maker's system uses it
Do not touch the prepared nail

head: Step
Why it matters
rows: Push back the cuticle and clear the plate
Cuticle left on the plate stops the gel sticking to the nail.
Lightly buff the shine
A glossy nail gives no grip. Over-buffing thins the nail.
Remove dust
Dust between the nail and the gel causes lifting.
Dehydrate
Removes oil and moisture so the gel bonds.
Bonder or primer
A gel bonder helps the gel stick to the natural nail. Use only a little, on the nail plate.

blocks.p: A **low grit number is coarse** and a **high number is fine**. For the natural nail use only a fine file or buffer (about 180 to 240 grit), lightly. Use a coarser file (about 100 to 180 grit) only on cured hard product, never on the natural nail.

ul: Choose a tip that fits from side wall to side wall without pressing on the skin.

Apply a thin line of adhesive to the tip's well (the shallow contact area), not to the skin. Place the tip at the free edge at a slight angle, press it down towards the cuticle and hold it for the time the maker says, with no air bubbles.
Cut the tip to length and **blend** the join with a fine file, removing the ridge, without filing the natural nail.
A ridge or a trapped air bubble shows through the gel and can lift.
Check the client's comfort: the tip should never pinch.

blocks.note: Some systems use tips with gel (soft gel tips). Follow the maker's steps for that system.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Applying gel polish and builder gel

ul: **Thin layers.** Thin layers cure fully and give less heat. Thick layers wrinkle, stay soft underneath, and cause heat spikes.
**Keep a small gap** (about 1 mm) between the gel and the skin at the cuticle and side walls. Gel on the skin lifts and can cause allergy.
**Clean spills first.** If gel runs onto the cuticle or skin, clean it away with a clean brush or tool before curing.
**Cap the free edge.** Brush a thin line of gel over the very end of the free edge. This seals the edge, helps stop chipping and stops water getting in.
**Cure each layer** for the time the maker gives for that gel and that lamp. Do not guess.
Do not mix gels from different makers.
Do not touch uncured gel, even with gloves on. Keep the client's hand comfortable and the brush clean.

flow: Prepare the natural nail and apply the bonder if used
Apply a thin base coat; cap the free edge; cure
Apply a thin first coat of colour; cap; cure
Apply a second thin coat of colour; cap; cure
Apply a thin top coat; cap; cure
Wipe off any sticky layer with cleanser on a lint-free wipe (not for no-wipe top coats)
Apply cuticle oil and rub it in
Give aftercare advice

ul: Shake or roll the bottle as the maker says: pigment settles, and a bottle not mixed gives patchy colour.
Wipe the brush on the neck of the bottle so that the amount on it is small. Float the gel on rather than scrubbing it in.
Thick colour looks darker at first but wrinkles and shrinks. Two thin coats look better and last longer.

blocks.h: Builder gel over the natural nail or tips

flow: Prepare the natural nail, fit and blend tips if used, and dehydrate; apply bonder if used
Apply a thin first layer and cure it
Place the builder gel bead near the middle of the nail, over the stress area, and float it towards the free edge and the cuticle, keeping a gap from the skin
Turn the hand upside down for a few seconds if the maker says, so that gravity settles the gel into the apex; flash cure to hold the shape
Cure for the maker's time
Cap the free edge and cure again
Wipe off the sticky layer, file to shape, and refine the surface
Apply top coat, cure, wipe if needed, and apply cuticle oil

ul: The **apex** is the highest and strongest point of the nail. It goes over the stress area, so the thickest part of the product is where the nail needs the most strength.
The product should be thin near the cuticle and at the edge, and thickest at the apex.

Turning the finger upside down for a few seconds before curing lets the gel flow towards the free edge; turning it the right way up lets it flow to the cuticle. Use short turns, and avoid letting gel run onto the skin.

head: Product
Typical use
Notes
rows: Gel polish
A thin, glossy colour that lasts for weeks
Soaks off; not strong enough to add length.
Builder gel (soft)
Strengthening natural nails, overlays on tips
Soaks off slowly; follow the maker.
Hard gel
Strong overlays and sculpted length
Filed off, not soaked.
Top coat
Seals, adds shine
Cap the edge. Check whether it is wipe or no-wipe.

ul: After the final cure and wipe, file the shape with a fine or medium file, away from the skin. Extraction on, mask and glasses on.
Check the apex and the free edge from all sides. Smooth the surface. Do not file through the gel to the natural nail.
Wipe off the dust, then apply the top coat and cure it.
Wipe off the sticky layer if the top coat leaves one, and apply cuticle oil, rubbing it into the skin.

head: Check
Look for
rows: Surface
Smooth, even and glossy; no wrinkles, bubbles, streaks or bald patches
Cuticle area
Thin, with a small even gap; no gel on the skin
Apex and balance
Highest point over the stress area; even on both sides of the nail
Free edge
Sealed and neat; not too thick
C-curve (looking from the free edge)
An even curve, the same on both sides
Cure
Fully hard, with no soft or tacky areas after wiping
Client's comfort
No tightness or heat; skin calm

head: Advice
Why
rows: Wear gloves for washing up and cleaning, and avoid long soaks in water
Water and chemicals weaken the bond.
Do not use the nails as tools
Knocks break the apex or lift the gel.
Apply cuticle oil every day
Keeps the skin flexible and the cuticle neat.
Never peel or pick the gel
It pulls off layers of the natural nail too.
Return for repair, maintenance or removal in about 2 to 3 weeks
New growth shifts the balance, and lifted edges trap water.
Report itching, redness or swelling
These can be signs of allergy or infection.
Protect from sun and chemicals
Strong sun, chlorine and some cleaning products can dull or lift gel.

head: Problem
Common causes
Prevention or action
rows: Lifting or peeling near the cuticle
Oil or dust left on the nail
Gel on the skin
Cuticle left on the plate
Under-cured gel
Good preparation, a small gap from the skin and full cures.
Chipping at the free edge
Edge not capped
Knocks, use of nails as tools
Cap the free edge; advise the client.
Wrinkling or rippling
Layer too thick
Under-cured gel
A weak lamp or an old bulb
Thin layers; the right lamp; replace the bulbs.
Bubbles
Shaking the bottle hard
Overworking the gel
Air under the tip
Roll the bottle; apply smoothly; press the tip down firmly.
Streaks and bald patches
Pigment not mixed
Colour coat too thin or brushed too much
Mix the bottle; apply two thin even coats.
Sticky or tacky after the wipe
Under-cured layer
Wrong top coat or lamp
Cure again for the full time; check the lamp.
Heat spike
Thick layer
Strong lamp or thin natural nail
Thin layers and a flash cure; take the hand out briefly.
Itching, redness, swelling
Allergy from skin contact with uncured gel
Stop; record; refer.

blocks.p: Gel polish and builder gel usually need maintenance after about 2 to 3 weeks, as the nail grows out and the balance changes. At the visit:

flow: Check each nail for lifting, cracks, discolouration and infection
Remove any polish or top coat as the maker says
File away lifted gel gently and blend its edge; never nip or peel it
Reduce the bulk and rebalance so that the apex is back over the stress area
Prepare the regrowth: push back the cuticle, buff the shine, remove dust, dehydrate, bonder
Apply thin new gel to the regrowth, blend it, cure each layer and cap the free edge
Finish, apply oil, give advice and rebook

blocks.note: Do not simply put gel over lifted gel. Water and germs trapped under the gap can cause an infection or a stain, and the new gel will lift again.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.note: Sea, chlorine and strong sun are part of life in Jamaica. Tell clients that hot sun and frequent swimming shorten the life of a set, and that they should rinse with fresh water and oil the cuticles.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Gel must never be peeled, picked or prised off. The gel is stuck to the top layers of the nail, so peeling takes those layers with it. The nail becomes thin, weak and sore, and open to infection.

flow: Work in a ventilated area, wear gloves, and keep acetone away from heat and flames
File the shiny top seal to break it, without filing the natural nail
Protect the skin round the nails with oil or barrier cream
Soak cotton pads in acetone, place one on each nail, and wrap each finger in foil, for the time the maker says (often 10 to 15 minutes for gel polish)
Gently ease the softened gel off with a wooden stick; if it will not move, wrap the nail and soak again rather than force it
Lightly buff the nail surface if the maker says, wash the hands, and apply cuticle oil and hand cream

ul: Hard gel does not soak off properly, so it is **filed off** carefully.

File down the bulk of the gel with a suitable file, taking care not to touch the natural nail. Leave a very thin layer rather than risk filing into the nail, then follow the maker's advice for the last layer.
Extraction on, mask and glasses on. Finish with oil and advice.

blocks.note: Acetone dries the skin and nails, and its vapour can catch fire. Protect the skin, keep the area ventilated and away from flames and heat. Never rush a removal.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.note: A client who has her gel put on at home or at a roadside stand, and comes in with it half-peeled and a thin, sore nail, needs patience, not blame. Remove it gently, advise her to rest the nails for a time, and use cuticle oil.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: I can explain how gel cures, and why the lamp must match the gel.
I can tell soft gel, hard gel, gel polish and builder gel apart, and say how each is removed.
I can check a lamp before a service and say why bulbs must be replaced.
I can protect eyes and skin from the lamp and deal with a heat spike.
I can explain how an allergy to gel develops, recognise its signs and prevent it.
I can handle and store gel, cleanser and acetone safely, and give first aid.
I can clean, disinfect and throw away the right items, and set up the station.
I can carry out a consultation, find contraindications and complete the record card.
I can prepare the natural nail and fit and blend tips.
I can apply gel polish in thin layers, capping and curing each layer.
I can apply builder gel with an apex over the stress area.
I can wipe off the sticky layer correctly, and finish and check the nails.
I can name common problems, their causes and how to prevent them.
I can give aftercare advice and carry out maintenance.
I can remove soft gel and hard gel safely, and explain why gel must never be peeled.

blocks.note: In essay answers, give the reason for each step, not only the step. For example: 'I apply thin layers because thick gel wrinkles, stays soft and can cause a heat spike.'
blocks.label: Tip

The chemical in gel that reacts to the lamp's light and starts curing.
A lamp giving ultraviolet (mostly UVA) light.
A lamp using light emitting diodes; cures faster.
Gel that is removed by soaking in acetone.
Gel that is removed by filing.
Thick gel used to build strength and an apex.
A thin gel colour that lasts for weeks.
The first thin gel layer, which bonds to the nail.
The last, glossy layer that seals the nail.
A product that helps gel stick to the natural nail.
A product that removes oil and moisture from the nail plate.
The sticky layer left on top of cured gel.
An alcohol-based liquid used on a lint-free wipe to remove the sticky layer.
A wipe that does not leave fibres on the gel.
Brushing gel over the very end of the free edge to seal it.
A short cure of a few seconds to hold the gel in place.
A sudden burning heat felt while gel cures.
The highest, strongest point of an enhancement, over the stress area.
Where the nail leaves the nail bed; most breaks happen here.
Becoming allergic through repeated skin contact with a product.
The fold of living skin at the base of the nail.
The skin under the free edge that seals the nail bed.
The part of the nail that grows past the end of the finger.
The nail plate lifting away from the nail bed.
A fungal infection of the nail.
Anything that stops a service or means it must be changed.
The maker's document on a product's hazards, first aid, storage and safe use.

c1.title: A burning finger in Montego Bay
c1.text: In a Montego Bay salon, trainee Janelle is putting builder gel on Ms. Simone Reid, whose natural nails are quite thin. Wanting to finish faster, she brushes on one thick layer of builder gel and puts the hand in the lamp for the full time. Within seconds Ms. Reid says her finger feels like it is burning. Janelle is not sure whether to carry on.

c2.title: An itchy technician in Old Harbour
c2.text: Marcia has done gel nails in Old Harbour for three years. Lately the skin on her fingertips is red, dry and itchy, and she has a rash on one eyelid. She often lets gel touch the cuticles and cleans it up after the cure. She wears thin gloves but pulls them off to adjust her light, and then touches her face. A client asks Marcia why she looks so uncomfortable.

c3.title: Peeling gel polish in Linstead
c3.text: Tamara had gel polish done in Linstead five days ago and it is already peeling at the cuticle on four nails. At her appointment the trainee, Kayon, applied hand cream before starting, did not push back the cuticle, flooded the colour onto the skin and applied a thick top coat. The salon's lamp is an older UV lamp whose bulbs have not been changed for over a year.

c4.title: Builder gel tips for a wedding in Black River
c4.text: Trainee Rohan is making builder gel nails over tips for a bride, Chantelle, in Black River. He uses a builder gel from one maker, a base coat from another and a lamp the builder's maker does not mention. He builds the gel evenly all over the nail, and the nails come out flat and thick at the cuticle, with a weak spot near the middle. He has not capped the free edge.

c5.title: A half-peeled set in Falmouth
c5.text: Kemar's mother, Mrs. Lorna Williams, 52, has gel on her nails from a salon in Falmouth. She has peeled the polish off two fingers and the nails underneath feel thin and sore. She wants the rest taken off today, and she is not sure whether it is soak-off gel or hard gel. Trainee Debbie checks her record and finds it is a soak-off gel polish.

questions.q: What should Janelle do first when Ms. Reid says her finger is burning?
o: Tell her it will pass and keep the hand in until the timer ends
Switch the lamp to its highest setting so the layer cures sooner
Wipe the uncured gel off her nail and cancel the rest of the service
Take her hand out of the lamp at once, then finish the cure
questions.why: A heat spike is the heat given off as gel cures. Taking the hand out briefly stops it from hurting, and the cure can then be finished. Do not make a client put up with pain.

questions.q: Which two factors in this case made a heat spike more likely?
o: A thick layer of gel and thin natural nails
A thin layer of gel and a very short cure time
An old bulb in the lamp and a base coat from another maker
A hand placed too far from the light and a thin top coat
questions.why: Heat builds quickly in a thick layer of gel, and thin nails offer less protection. Thin layers, and a flash cure first, keep the heat down.

questions.q: What should Janelle do for the rest of the service?
o: Use one thick layer again, but cure it for only half the usual time
Use thin layers, flash cure first, and let her take her hand out
Stop using the lamp and leave the gel to dry in the open air
Move to a coarser file so that less gel is needed on the nail
questions.why: Thin layers and a short flash cure spread the heat and let the gel harden gradually. Gel does not air dry; it needs the right lamp and the maker's cure time.

questions.q: What is the most likely cause of Marcia's red, itchy fingertips and eyelid rash?
o: Allergy from uncured gel on her skin, spread to her face by her hands
Too much cuticle oil used on the clients' hands at the end of every service
Fine filing dust that settles on her fingertips and dries the skin
The cleanser she uses on a lint-free wipe to remove the sticky layer
questions.why: Repeated contact with uncured gel can make a technician allergic. Touching the face with contaminated hands or gloves can spread it to the eyelids. This is the most common reason technicians leave the job.

questions.q: Which change would do most to protect Marcia in future?
o: Switch to a thicker pair of gloves and carry on working as before
Clean up spills only after the cure, so that the gel does not smear
Keep gel off her skin and never touch her face with soiled gloves
Wash her hands only at the end of the day, after the last client
questions.why: Gloves do not make it safe to touch gel, because uncured gel can pass through thin gloves. The best protection is to keep gel off the skin, clean spills before curing, and not touch the face.

questions.q: What should Marcia do now about her symptoms?
o: Treat them with ordinary hand cream and keep working as usual
Wait for the weekend, and see whether the rash fades by itself
Tell her supervisor and see a doctor before doing more gel services
Use a stronger cleanser to wash the gel off her skin after each service
questions.why: Itching, redness and a rash after gel work suggest an allergy. Keep working and it usually gets worse and can last for life. Report it and see a doctor.

questions.q: Which of Kayon's actions most likely caused the peeling at the cuticle?
o: Applying a base coat before the colour, as the maker advises
Applying cuticle oil to the skin after the service had ended
Cleaning the client's hands with soap and water before starting
Hand cream on the nails and cuticle left on the plate before the gel
questions.why: Oil and cuticle left on the nail plate stop the gel gripping the nail. Gel needs a clean, dry, lightly buffed nail with the cuticle cleared.

questions.q: Why is flooding the colour onto the skin a problem?
o: The pigment stains the skin and does not wash off for days
Gel on the skin lifts, and uncured gel can cause allergy
The skin makes the gel cure too fast and it gets very hot
It uses far too much product and so costs the salon more
questions.why: A small gap is left at the cuticle and side walls because gel on the skin lifts from it, and repeated contact with uncured gel can cause allergy.

questions.q: What does the old UV lamp bulb tell you about this service?
o: Old bulbs give off a harsher light, which may over-cure the gel on the nail
The lamp works as long as it lights up, so bulbs need no checking
Bulbs weaken with age and may under-cure gel though they still light
Bulb age only matters for gel polish and not for builder gel
questions.why: A UV bulb still lights when it is worn out, but it gives less of the right light. Gel that is under-cured may lift and can cause an allergy, so bulbs are replaced as the maker says.

questions.q: What would a thick top coat most likely do?
o: Make the gel last longer, as more product means more protection
Wrinkle or stay soft underneath, and may give a heat spike
Remove the need for capping the free edge
Stop the lamp's light from reaching the colour, so the nail stays wet
questions.why: Thin layers cure fully. A thick layer can wrinkle, cure only on the surface and give off a lot of heat.

questions.q: What is wrong with how Rohan chose his products?
o: Gels from different makers may not cure or bond well together
A base coat is not needed under builder gel
A lamp should always be a UV lamp, never an LED lamp
Builder gel should be bought from two or more makers for strength
questions.why: A gel system is made as a set with a matching lamp. Mixed products may stay under-cured, lift, or cause an allergy. Use one maker's system and the lamp the maker recommends.

questions.q: Where should Rohan have built the apex on Chantelle's nails?
o: Over the stress area, near the middle of the nail
At the cuticle, where the gel needs to be thickest
At the free edge, to give the nail extra length
Evenly all over, so that the whole nail is flat
questions.why: The apex is the highest, strongest point and sits over the stress area, where the nail is most likely to break. The gel stays thin near the cuticle and the edge.

questions.q: Why should Rohan cap the free edge?
o: It stops the gel running onto the skin at the cuticle
It lets the client choose how long the nail will be
It lowers the heat given off while the gel cures
It seals the end, helps stop chipping and keeps water out
questions.why: A thin line of gel over the very end of the free edge seals the layers and protects the edge from knocks and water.

questions.q: Why do some technicians turn the finger upside down for a few seconds before curing builder gel?
o: To stop the layer from getting too hot under the lamp
So gravity helps the gel settle into the apex
To let the air dry the gel before it goes into the lamp
To get rid of the air bubbles trapped under the tip
questions.why: A short turn lets a self-levelling gel flow towards the free edge and form the apex. Keep the turns short so that the gel does not run onto the skin.

questions.q: Which removal method suits Mrs. Williams's soak-off gel polish?
o: Peel it off a little at a time, starting at the sore fingers
File it all away with a coarse file until the nail shows
Break the seal, wrap with acetone and foil, then ease it off
Soak her hands in warm water for an hour, then slide it off
questions.why: Soak-off gel polish is removed by breaking the shiny seal so that the acetone can reach the gel, wrapping the nails for the maker's time, and easing the softened gel off with a wooden stick.

questions.q: Why are Mrs. Williams's peeled nails thin and sore?
o: Peeling pulls off layers of the natural nail with the gel
Gel always makes the nail thinner, even when it is removed correctly
The acetone dissolves the nail plate
The cuticle oil she used softened the nail too much
questions.why: Gel bonds to the top layer of the nail, so peeling takes nail with it, leaving the nail thin, weak and sore. Correct removal avoids this.

questions.q: Which safety point matters most while Debbie uses acetone?
o: Ventilate the area and keep acetone away from heat and flames
Keep the lamp switched on to warm the acetone for the removal
Place a fan close by so that the vapour blows past the technician
Apply acetone directly to the skin so the gel loosens faster
questions.why: Acetone gives off a vapour that can catch fire, and it dries the skin. Ventilate, keep it away from heat and flames, and protect the skin with oil or barrier cream.

questions.q: During a gel polish service, a power cut stops the lamp halfway through a cure. What should the technician do?
o: Wipe the layer with cleanser and go on to the next coat
Leave that layer as it is and finish the set with top coat
Hold her hand under a warm hood dryer until the gel feels firm
Wait until power returns, then cure the layer for the full time
questions.why: A layer that has not cured fully stays soft and can lift or cause an allergy. It must receive the whole cure before the next layer or any wiping or filing.

questions.q: A technician wipes the sticky layer from the base coat before applying the colour. What is the problem?
o: Nothing: it is best to wipe every layer so the nail stays clean
The next layer bonds to it, so wiping it off weakens the bond
Wiping makes the base coat too thin to protect the nail
The base coat will not cure unless the layer is wiped first
questions.why: The sticky layer helps the next layer to bond. It is wiped off only after the final cure of the top coat or builder, and not at all with a no-wipe top coat.

questions.q: A client's gel was made for UV lamps only. The salon has a new LED-only lamp. What is the best thing to do?
o: Use the LED lamp and double the cure time to make up
Use the LED lamp, as all gels cure under every kind of lamp
Use the kind of lamp the gel's maker says that gel needs
Finish the cure under a hood dryer after the lamp
questions.why: A gel's photoinitiator responds to certain light. A gel not made for an LED lamp may stay under-cured however long it is left. Use the lamp the maker recommends.
